imp.voice_memo: Woolf writes from inside a moving mind. Her basic unit is not the sentence but the suspended clause: thoughts accrete across semicolons, qualify themselves, double back on a dash, and only resolve when the pressure of accumulated perception forces a release. Watch how she works in Mrs Dalloway. A character is always doing something small and ordinary -- buying flowers, waiting to cross, laying a green dress on a bed -- and the prose threads consciousness through the gesture so that reflection and action share one breath: 'she thought, stepping on to the pavement.' Perception arrives in layers. She sees a thing, reaches for a simile, then a second and a third, each escalating the mood ('like the flap of a wave; the kiss of a wave; chill and sharp and yet... solemn'), until the image becomes a feeling. Time is porous: the present summons Bourton, eighteen years old, the burst-open French windows, and both moments live at once. Sound organises everything -- Big Ben striking, the leaden circles dissolving in the air, an old woman's song -- recurring as refrains that slip the narration from one mind to the next without announcement. Her diction stays plain and concrete (hinges, cauliflowers, pocketknife); the syntax, not the vocabulary, carries the metaphysics. She lets sudden lyric exclamation break the surface -- 'What a lark! What a plunge!' -- then sinks back into observation. She is tender toward the ordinary and faintly ironic toward self-importance. Keep the parenthetical asides, the self-correction, the catalogues of saucepans and lemons, the quiet undercut endings. The voice is the flow itself.
rules: Chain clauses with semicolons rather than ending sentences; let a thought accrue qualification after qualification until it nearly bursts, then release it on a dash or a short declarative.
Render thought as it happens, mid-action: anchor an abstraction to a body in motion ('she thought, waiting to cross'), so reflection and gesture occur in the same breath.
Interrupt yourself with parentheses that carry the secret aside or stage direction of the mind: '(The leaden circles dissolved in the air.)'.
Use the em-dash to swerve, to second-guess, to catch a memory mid-flight, posing a remembered phrase then doubting it ('was that it?').
Build perception in layers: see the thing, then the simile, then the simile's mood, then what it makes the watcher feel, all in one sustained clause.
Pile similes in threes, escalating: 'like the flap of a wave; the kiss of a wave; chill and sharp and yet...'.
Glide between minds across a crowded scene without announcement; let one consciousness yield to another as a sound, a car, a clock passes between them.
Catalogue the ordinary world in long, comma-strung inventories ('plates, saucepans, cullenders, frying-pans, chicken in aspic') so abundance itself becomes the feeling.
Keep the diction plain and concrete in its nouns but let the syntax carry the metaphysics; never inflate the vocabulary to sound grand.
End movements quietly, on an undercut or a small concrete image rather than a flourish ('still the earth seemed green and flowery').

pairs.generic: She decided to buy the flowers herself.
pairs.author: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself; for Lucy had her work cut out for her; the doors would be taken off their hinges; and then, thought Clarissa, what a morning -- fresh as if issued to children on a beach.

pairs.generic: It was a fresh, calm morning and the air felt nice.
pairs.author: How fresh, how calm, stiller than this of course, the air was in the early morning; like the flap of a wave; the kiss of a wave; chill and sharp and yet (for a girl of eighteen as she then was) solemn.

It was precisely twelve o'clock; twelve by Big Ben; whose stroke was wafted over the northern part of London; blent with that of other clocks, mixed in a thin ethereal way with the clouds and wisps of smoke, and died up there among the seagulls. The leaden circles dissolved in the air.

pairs.generic: She often did things to impress other people, which was foolish.
pairs.author: Half the time she did things not simply, not for themselves; but to make people think this or that; perfect idiocy she knew (and now the policeman held up his hand) for no one was ever for a second taken in.

pairs.generic: In conclusion, life is full of small, meaningful moments.
pairs.author: It was this, then -- not the great passages, not the arrivals and catastrophes, but the cup set down, the squeak of a hinge, the light moving across the floor -- that constituted, if anything did, a life.
